narrative:
The model estimates a 61% chance that you will leave your current role, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key factors that, in combination, signal a higher risk of departure compared to colleagues who are expected to stay.

The strongest influence comes from the fact that you have received other job opportunities while at the company. Most employees who are predicted to stay (77%) have not received such offers; having them makes the model see you as more likely to leave. The second most important factor is that you have participated in only 1–3 training programs in the last three years. This is roughly average, yet the model interprets the relatively low number as reducing your attachment to the organization and slightly increasing the likelihood you will move on. Finally, your overall career experience of 6–10 years also contributes. While this is common among those expected to stay (35% of that group), the model sees mid-level experience as a point where employees often begin exploring external options.

Taken together, these three elements outweigh the many positive aspects of your profile, such as high emotional commitment, strong recognition, and satisfaction with rewards. The organization should discuss retention measures with you, such as clearer promotion paths or additional development opportunities. You may wish to reflect on whether the external offers align with your long-term goals.
